This game has been a huge hit everywhere I have played it. I really hope I can bring something very fun to Voat as well. The rules are incredibly simple:

  • I will post a picture of 3 creatures. You take one of the creatures and edit the picture in a program of your choice (always save as .png)
  • When you edit the picture, you 'evolve' the creature. This can be a new limb, sensory organ, tail, etc.
  • Post the picture here. If it has the same name it is an evolution of said creature. If it has a new name it is a subspecies. For example - if a creature called a "X" is edited and someone names the new edit a "Xo" both the X and Xo exist. But if the new creature is still called "X" it replaces the original X and the original X cannot be evolved again.
  • If you are editing someone's creature, reply to their post
  • You may edit any creature you want, but you cannot edit the same creature twice in a row.
  • There is no winning or losing, just having fun. Our goal is to create a fun new world full of creatures, not be an internet tough guy.

Still confused - here's an example.

Let's begin. We are in a small pool. There is no other life around but ourselves. 3 creatures dominate this pool:

  • Sy - A algae that just floats around gathering sunlight for energy
  • Cip - Feeds on Sy. It is very fast.
  • Roh - A voracious, yet inefficient predator. It whirls through the pool hoping to grab a Cip with its claws.

Current evolution tree

Feel free to ask any questions. And let's have some fun, huh? The last big game I had resulted in this.

The Mathematical Editing of Sergio Leone's 'The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly'
Wow, never realized that the editing itself could have an effect like that. how much of it do you think was the director's decision on set, versus decisions made post-production?

Based on very little actual information and mostly just personal belief, I speculate that the director probably had an idea of how he wanted to scene to turn out and visualized it fairly close to how it ended up- usually storyboards are worked on for a while to basically map out the entire film from beginning to end- so he most likely wanted that sequence to turn out that way. However he clearly couldn't account for the timing of it very accurately in story boards as they are literal pictures so most likely the timing of each shot was done in post production whereas the sequencing was done prior. Again I'm sure that he knew that the pacing would increase as the sequence went on so he probably made those sorts of notes but in the end while watching the product come together I assume he had to fine tune the timing with the editor. I've made significantly less impressive sequencing in my editing and had an idea for how I wanted those sequences to look time wise however when I got to the editing page I realized some of my ideas were off base from what would actually work for the sequences so I had to make adjustments.

Summarily I think the director knew he wanted the scene to turn out the way it did so on set he worked on making sure all of the shots he would need were ready and available. The cutting of the shots together most likely was based on a sketch of the sequence that was predetermined. In the editing room the timing and flow of the scene was probably fine tuned around that original baseline.

Again these are only my presumptions based on no actual knowledge of how Sergio Leone actually works on his films.
